The Sector Skills Council for Building in Nigeria has directed construction companies and property developers to suspend non-essential heavy outdoor work between noon and 3:30 pm and introduce mandatory rest and hydration breaks to protect workers from extreme heat. The council warned that rising temperatures, prolonged dry spells, dusty conditions and flash flooding were exposing construction workers to heatstroke, respiratory illnesses and workplace accidents, with potential consequences for productivity and workers’ livelihoods. In a national safety advisory issued on Tuesday, the council directed contractors to restructure working hours, provide adequate drinking water and establish shaded resting areas at construction sites across the country. The advisory, signed by the council’s President, Samson Opaluwah, identified roofing, concrete pouring, manual excavation and scaffolding as some of the labour-intensive activities that should be avoided during peak heat periods. The advisory read, “Building Skills Constructing managers-operating primarily in open-air environments-face severe health, safety, and productivity risks. All licensed construction entities and property developers are hereby instructed to integrate the mandatory operational controls outlined below to safeguard workers’ health, ensure site integrity, and maintain national productivity standards.” It recommended that contractors move such activities to early morning hours between 6 am and 10:30 am or late afternoons, with adequate lighting where work extends into the night. The council said workers should also receive mandatory five- to 10-minute hydration breaks every 20 minutes, while clean drinking water must be provided within 50 metres of every active work area. “Peak Solar Avoidance: All site contractors must eliminate non-essential heavy manual labour (e.g., concrete pouring, manual digging, scaffolding, roofing work) during peak heat hours between 12:00 PM and 3:30 PM. Workers must be granted mandatory 5-10-minute hydration breaks every 20 minutes. Electrolytes & First Aid: Site clinics/first aid stations must be stocked with Oral Rehydration Salts and cooling media (ice packs, wet towels) for rapid response to acute heat distress,” it added. It further directed construction companies to provide first-aid facilities stocked with oral rehydration salts, ice packs and wet towels to respond to cases of heat exhaustion. 89% of Nigerians support methane emission cuts — Survey EFCC vows crackdown on sponsors of illegal mining El Niño: Prepare for heat wave, Ekiti tells farmers The directive comes amid growing concerns about the impact of extreme weather conditions on outdoor workers, particularly in the construction industry, where employees are routinely exposed to direct sunlight while performing physically demanding tasks. According to the council, prolonged exposure to high temperatures could cause dehydration, heat cramps and potentially fatal heatstroke. It warned that heat-related illnesses could also affect workers’ concentration and reaction times, increasing the likelihood of falls from scaffolding, machinery-related accidents and injuries from falling construction materials. The advisory stated that dry weather conditions could increase airborne dust, exposing workers involved in excavation, block-making and cement mixing to respiratory illnesses, including occupational asthma and silicosis. It also identified stagnant water from irregular rainfall and poorly drained construction sites as potential mosquito breeding grounds, increasing the risk of malaria and worker absenteeism. The council also warned that poorly planned work stoppages could reduce the earnings of daily-paid artisans, urging contractors to adjust schedules rather than leave workers without income during extreme weather conditions. On protective equipment, it directed contractors to provide breathable high-visibility clothing, safety helmets fitted with neck shades and ultraviolet-protective eyewear. Workers must also receive N95 or higher-grade dust masks during dusty conditions, while unpaved access roads, demolition areas and exposed earth surfaces should be regularly wetted to suppress dust. The council further instructed construction companies to introduce a buddy system under which workers monitor one another for symptoms of heat stress, including dizziness, confusion, slurred speech and unusual sweating patterns. It directed site health and safety officers to monitor daily weather forecasts issued by the Nigerian Meteorological Agency and adjust work schedules according to prevailing conditions. The advisory also requires contractors to conduct 10-minute morning safety briefings covering heat stress, disease prevention and emergency response procedures. The council said it would conduct unannounced inspections in collaboration with relevant professional regulatory bodies, including the Council of Registered Builders of Nigeria and the Nigerian Institute of Building, as well as the Federal Ministry of Housing and Urban Development. It warned that contractors who failed to provide adequate worker protection could face regulatory sanctions, safety citations or temporary suspension of construction activities. The directive cited the National Building Code, the Builders Registration Act, the Labour Act and the Employees’ Compensation Act 2010 as the legal frameworks supporting its intervention.
